_notes: Dominican formation, the novitiate and the studium's philosophy years. E3 §5.1: clothing, the bell, the chant, the vow, the library at night, the two professors, the doubt, the Lay Dominicans, the evaluation letter.

events.title: The First Fortnight
events.body: The postulancy is two weeks that pretend to be a year: the house's rhythm learned at speed, the Office followed with a finger, the names of eleven men and the faults of nine. {@novice_master} watches everything and says almost nothing, and on the tenth day he says one thing: that a man who wants to know whether he is called should stop asking and start getting up, and that the bell will tell him. The bell is at five-twenty. You have been up at four every day, waiting for it.

choices.label: Sleep until the bell; the waiting is its own kind of pride
choices.outcome: You sleep. The bell wakes you and you are in the stall on time and no earlier, and the novice master, who had noticed the four o'clock light under your door, notices its absence, and says, at the end of the fortnight, that you have begun.

choices.label: Keep the four o'clock; the hour is yours
choices.outcome: The hour is yours all year. The novice master says nothing about it. It is a real hour and it costs you at recreation, where you fall asleep, and the house, which is kind, lets you.

events.title: The Novice Master's Bad Day
events.body: {@novice_master} is a good man with one flaw, and today it is out: something at the provincial's office, a letter, and he has been short with three novices before Terce and unjust with one, {@confrere}, who did nothing, and who is in the garden now, white, deciding whether he came to the wrong order. The novice master is in his room with the door shut. The Rule says a brother must ask pardon before sundown, and nobody has ever seen the novice master ask pardon of anyone.

choices.label: Go to the garden, and sit with the one who was wronged
choices.outcome: You say nothing useful and he is grateful for it. At Vespers the novice master is at his stall with a face like a man who has been to confession, and after supper he goes to the garden himself, and you leave them to it, and the novice stays.

choices.label: Knock on the novice master's door
choices.outcome: He opens it. He says he knows. He says he is going to the garden at Vespers and that he did not need a novice to tell him, and that he is glad one did, and both are true, and he is exact with you for a week and then not.

choices.label: Say nothing; it is the novice master's house
choices.outcome: The novice master goes to the garden on his own, at sundown, as the Rule asks, and the house sees it, and the novice stays, and you learn that a house corrects itself sometimes, and that you were not needed, which is also a lesson.

events.title: Learning the Tones
events.body: The novitiate sings the Office in the order's own chant, which is not quite the chant the parishes know, and you cannot sing it. Not badly: not at all. The cantor, a novice a year ahead, has been asked to teach you in the hour after None, and he is patient in the way of men who have been told to be, and on the third day he says, gently, that some men are given to the choir and some to the pulpit, and that the order has room for both, and it is not a compliment.

choices.label: Work at it every day until Advent, whatever it costs
choices.outcome: It costs the free hour every day until Advent. By Advent you can sing the tones, plainly, in tune, without joy, and the cantor says it is enough, and the old friars, who have heard every novice for forty years, say you learned it, which is what they say of the ones who did.

choices.label: Accept the pulpit and mouth the choir
choices.outcome: You mouth it for seven years. Nobody minds. It is a small dishonesty at the heart of the day and you notice it every morning, and at your first priorship the house you govern sings badly and you know why.

choices.label: Ask the old cantor, the one who is eighty, instead
choices.outcome: He teaches you in a week what the young one could not in a month, since he has taught sixty novices, and he says the young cantor is a better singer and a worse teacher and that both will be needed, and you have a friend among the old men.

events.title: Visiting Sunday
events.body: Once a term the novitiate lets families in: a Sunday afternoon in the parlour, tea, the habit on show, and your mother at the door with a bag of things you are not allowed to have and your father in the car, since he has said he will come in when he is ready and is not. Your mother says you look thin. She says the novice master seems kind. She says, quietly, when the room is loud, that your father does not understand it and is trying, and that she does not either and has stopped trying, and that she is proud.

choices.label: Go out to the car
choices.outcome: He is listening to the game. You sit in the passenger seat in the habit and listen to it with him for the fourth quarter, and he says at the end that the house looks well kept, and that is all, and it is everything, and he comes in the next term.

choices.label: Stay with your mother; she is the one who came in
choices.outcome: She talks for an hour and you listen, and she is glad, and at the end she says your father will come in when he comes in, and he does, two terms later, on his own, and stands in the chapel and does not sit.

choices.label: Ask the novice master whether you may keep one thing from the bag
choices.outcome: He says one. You choose. It is a photograph, and it is on your desk for forty years, and your mother, told, says she would have chosen the socks.

events.title: The Torn Habit
events.body: You have torn the habit, badly, on the garden fence, the first week you wore it, and the habit is the house's, and the house has four. {@novice_master} will see it at Vespers. The tailor comes on Thursdays. It is Monday. {@confrere} has offered to lend you his second, which he is not supposed to have, and the old brother who does the mending has offered to do it tonight, in silence, if you sit with him and hold the lamp.

choices.label: Sit with the old brother and hold the lamp
choices.outcome: It takes two hours. He tells you, in the great silence, which he breaks for it, about every novice who tore his habit in the first week, and there were many, and you are the first in a decade to hold the lamp, and he mends it so it does not show.

choices.label: Borrow the second habit and say nothing
choices.outcome: Nobody notices. The tailor mends yours Thursday. The second habit goes back, and {@confrere} and you have a secret, which in a novitiate is a bond and a risk, and the novice master, who notices everything, says nothing, which means he knows.

choices.label: Go to the novice master in the torn habit and say what happened
choices.outcome: He looks at the tear and says the fence has had a dozen habits and that the tailor comes Thursday and that in the meantime you will wear it torn, since it is the house's and the house can see it, and you do, and it is the best week of the year.

events.title: The Hour of Study in the Novitiate
events.body: The novitiate is not for study, the constitutions say, and gives it an hour a day anyway, and the hour is yours: the Fathers, the lives of the order's saints, the constitutions, or, since the novice master is not looking, the philosophy you will need at the studium. {@confrere} reads the saints. The old men read the Fathers. You have Aristotle under the constitutions and are not sure whether that is study or a lie.

choices.label: Read the order's saints, as the year asks
choices.outcome: You read them all. Some are dull and two are not, and one of the two changes how you pray, and the novice master, who asks each novice at Christmas what he has read, is pleased in a way he shows by asking nothing else.

choices.label: Read the Fathers, with the old men
choices.outcome: You read Augustine with a Dominican's suspicion and Chrysostom with none, and the old men, who read them every year, lend you their marked copies, and the marks are a second education.

choices.label: Read Aristotle under the constitutions
choices.outcome: You arrive at the studium a year ahead and the master of students notices in the first week. The novice master also noticed, in the novitiate, and said nothing, and says at your profession that he hopes the Ethics were worth it, and you are not sure.

events.title: One Vow
events.body: In the last month the novice master takes each novice alone and asks what he thinks he is about to vow. The order's profession is a single vow of obedience, understood to contain the others, and {@novice_master} has asked you why the order does it that way when every other order vows three, and has waited, and the answer in your head is the one from the constitutions, and he has heard that one from sixty novices.

choices.label: Say obedience is the vow that makes the others possible: a man who has given his will has nothing left to give
choices.outcome: He nods slowly and says that is the answer from the book, and that it is true, and that he would like to know whether you believe it, and you say you would like to know too, and he says that is the right answer for a man who is about to find out.

choices.label: Say Dominic vowed to the order, not to a list, and the order kept the shape
choices.outcome: He is delighted, since it is history and not theology, and asks where you read it, and tells you the rest, and the conversation is an hour, and it is the first time he has treated you as a man who will be a friar.

choices.label: Say you do not know, and that it frightens you
choices.outcome: He says that is the best answer he has had this year and that fear is the right thing to bring to the chapel in June, and that the men who were not afraid were the ones who left, and you profess in June, afraid, and it holds.

events.title: The Library at Night
events.body: The studium library closes at ten and nobody has ever enforced it, and the student brothers have divided, as students do, into the ones who leave at ten and the ones who are there at two, and the master of students has begun, this term, to walk through at midnight and write down names. It is not forbidden. It is noticed. {@confrere} is at the next table at one in the morning with the Prima Pars and a face like a man drowning in it.

choices.label: Stay; the Prima Pars will not read itself, and neither will his
choices.outcome: You are there at two, most nights, all year. The master of students writes your name eleven times and says nothing, and at the evaluation says you read more than the house's best and slept less than its worst, and both are on the file.

choices.label: Leave at ten, and be at Lauds with a face that has slept
choices.outcome: You are at Lauds every morning and the old men notice, and the reading is what it is, which is enough, and the master of students says at the evaluation that you keep the house's hours, which in a studium is rare praise.

choices.label: Take him out of the library at one and walk him round the cloister
choices.outcome: He talks for an hour about the article he cannot understand, and understands it by the end of the walk, and you understand it too, and it is how the two of you study for the next five years, at one in the morning, in the cloister.

events.title: The Two Professors
events.body: The studium has two professors of philosophy and they have not spoken since a footnote in the seventies. The student brothers take one or the other, in practice, and are marked accordingly, and the master of students, who was a student of one of them, pretends not to know. This term you have both. Each has assigned an essay on the same question and each expects the other's answer to be wrong, and both are due Friday, and you have one mind.

choices.label: Write two essays, one for each, honestly
choices.outcome: Both are marked well and neither professor speaks to you, since each has read the other's copy, and the master of students says at the evaluation that you were the first man in ten years to survive the pair, and it is on the file as a virtue.

choices.label: Write one essay, your own answer, and give it to both
choices.outcome: One marks it well and one does not, and the one who does not says in class that a student brother has taken sides, and the class knows which side, and you have a professor for life and an enemy for a term.

choices.label: Ask the master of students which to please
choices.outcome: He says neither, and both, and that the studium's purpose is to teach a man to think between two men who cannot, and he says it drily and you understand that it is the most useful thing he will say to you.

events.title: The Student Brothers' Sunday
events.body: The studium sends its student brothers to the priory church on Sunday afternoons to give a talk to the parish's adult catechesis, ten minutes each, on a subject the master of students assigns, and this Sunday the subject is yours and it is the Trinity, and the room is forty people who have had lunch. {@master_of_students} is at the back. It is the first time you will say a thing about God to people who did not have to come.

choices.label: Give them Thomas, the relations of origin, in ten minutes
choices.outcome: Six people understand and are transformed and thirty-four are asleep, and the master of students says afterward that it was correct and that you preached to the six, and that a Dominican has to decide whether the six are enough, and he has decided they are not.

choices.label: Give them a story about a family, and let the Trinity be in it
choices.outcome: Forty people understand something, and three of them have it wrong, and the master of students says afterward that the three are the price of the thirty-seven and that you will learn to lower the price, and he says it as a man who is pleased.

choices.label: Give them five minutes and take questions for five
choices.outcome: The questions are the talk. One of them you cannot answer and say so, and the room likes you for it more than for the minutes before, and the master of students writes that you can be honest in a pulpit, which he underlines.

events.title: A Summer in a Priory
events.body: The student brothers are sent for the summer to the province's priories, to live the life they are studying for, and you have been sent to one: eleven men, a parish, a city in July, a prior who has not had a student in five years and is not sure what to do with one. He has given you the hospital, since nobody wants it, and the eight o'clock Mass to serve at, and the rest of the day, he says, is yours, which in a priory means the house's.

choices.label: Take the hospital and be there every day
choices.outcome: It is four months of the dying. You learn more about the priesthood by August than in two years of the studium, and the prior writes to the master of students that the student brother was at the hospital more than the chaplain, and it is the beginning of a reputation.

choices.label: Take the house: the sacristy, the garden, the old men
choices.outcome: The prior is astonished and grateful. You learn the priory from the inside, which is the thing a studium cannot teach, and the old men write to the master of students, which they never do, to say send him back.

choices.label: Take the summer to read; the priory is quiet and the studium is not
choices.outcome: You read for four months in a cell with a fan, and the prior, who was hoping for help, says nothing and says it to the master of students, who says at the evaluation that a summer is a summer and that you spent yours on yourself.

events.title: The Article on the Existence of Evil
events.body: It is the third year and it is the question that undoes student brothers: not whether God exists, which the Five Ways handle for those who let them, but why this, why the child in the hospital, why the man on the stairs. Thomas has an answer and it is correct and it does not help. You have been in the chapel for an hour after Compline three nights running and {@master_of_students}, who has seen this every year for twenty, has left a note under your door that says only: my room, any hour.

choices.label: Go to his room, tonight
choices.outcome: He does not answer the question. He says nobody has and that the order was founded by a man who wept all night for sinners and did not have the answer either, and that the studium will give you the arguments and the chapel will give you the rest, and that you should keep going to both.

choices.label: Stay in the chapel, and let it be between you and God
choices.outcome: It takes a month. Something shifts that is not an answer. The master of students, who waited, says nothing when you stop going to the chapel after Compline, and writes on the file that you came through, and you did.

choices.label: Read the article again, harder, until the argument holds
choices.outcome: The argument holds. It is a real argument. It holds in the library and does not in the hospital, and you learn to carry both, and the master of students, told, says that is the Dominican settlement and that most men take longer to reach it.

events.title: The Lay Dominicans
events.body: The priory church has a chapter of Lay Dominicans, forty people who meet monthly, wear a scapular under their coats, and know the order's history better than the student brothers do. They have asked the studium for a brother to give them a talk on the constitutions, and the master of students has sent you, since you know them, and the forty people know more about the constitutions than you do and are polite about it for an hour.

choices.label: Let them teach you; ask them what the order looks like from outside
choices.outcome: They tell you, for two hours, and it is a view of the friars no friar has: which priories are loved, which priors are feared, what the parishes say. You go back every month for three years and the chapter adopts you, which is a real standing in the town.

choices.label: Teach them anyway; the constitutions have a shape they have not seen
choices.outcome: They have seen it. They are kind. The oldest member, a retired judge, corrects you on a date and you thank her and she says the last student brother argued, and asks you back, which is the judge's mercy.

choices.label: Ask them, at the end, whether any of them has a son
choices.outcome: Two of them do, and one of the sons is in the novitiate within three years, and the chapter says, at his profession, that the brother who asked was the one who thought of them as a family, which nobody had.

events.title: The Evaluation Letter
events.body: The studium writes to the provincial about each student brother every year, and the letter is read to the man, in the master of students' office, in full. Yours is being read now. It is fair. It says you read well and preach better and that the house finds you hard to know, and that the professed have said you are more at ease in the library than at recreation, and that this is a thing to watch in a Dominican, and {@master_of_students} has stopped reading and is looking at you.

choices.label: Say the letter is right
choices.outcome: He says most men argue with the letter and that the ones who do not are either honest or defeated, and asks which, and you say honest, and he writes one word on the letter before it goes, and the word is his, and you never see it.

choices.label: Say you will be at recreation every night until the letter is wrong
choices.outcome: You are. It is a penance and then it is not. The next letter says the house finds you easier to know, and the master of students reads that sentence twice, which is his way of saying it was noticed.

choices.label: Say the library is where a Dominican should be, and the house will manage
choices.outcome: He says the house will manage and that the order is made of men who thought so and of men who did not, and that both kinds become provincials, and only one kind is loved, and he does not say which, and you know.

events.title: The Modern Philosophers
events.body: The studium's philosophy is Thomist and the second year has a course on the moderns, taught by a young professor who was sent to a secular university for his doctorate and came back changed, and who has assigned Kant, and means it. The old professors have said at table that the course is a mistake. The young men have said it is the first air in the building. {@confrere} has stopped attending in protest, and the young professor has asked you, after class, whether you will stay.

choices.label: Stay, and read Kant as a Thomist reads him: to answer him
choices.outcome: You read him to answer him and find he is harder to answer than the old professors said, and the young professor says you are the first student who took him seriously enough to disagree, and you have a friend on the faculty and a reputation among the old ones.

choices.label: Leave with the protest; the studium is for Thomas
choices.outcome: The old professors approve. The young professor is transferred in two years and the course ends, and you are a Thomist who has not read Kant, which is a common thing and a smaller one, and you find it out in a pulpit fifteen years later.

choices.label: Stay, and tell the old professors why: Thomas would have read him
choices.outcome: One of them says Thomas read everyone and is silent, and the other says Thomas did not have to read Kant and neither do you, and you read him anyway, and the old professors are divided about you, which is the studium's highest compliment.

events.title: The Vigil Rota
events.body: The studium keeps an old custom: a brother in the chapel through the night before the great feasts, in turns, an hour each, from Compline to Lauds. The rota is on the board and the three o'clock hour is yours before Easter, and {@confrere}, who has the two o'clock, has asked whether you would take both, since he has a paper, and it is the kind of ask that a student brother makes once and a friar remembers.

choices.label: Take both hours
choices.outcome: Two hours in the dark before Easter with the tabernacle and the radiator. He finishes the paper. You do not tell anyone. He tells everyone, at recreation, that you took his hour, and the house's count of you rises in a way you did not do it for.

choices.label: Say no; the vigil is not a rota to be traded
choices.outcome: He is stung and does his hour and the paper is late and the master of students says nothing about the paper, and you are right, and he is a little further from you for a term, and it heals.

choices.label: Take his two o'clock and give him your three
choices.outcome: He is asleep by three and misses it. The chapel is empty for an hour before Easter, and the old brother who checks finds it so, and says nothing, and the two of you know, and it is a small thing you both carry.

events.title: The Provincial's Question
events.body: The provincial visits the studium once a year and sees each student brother for twenty minutes, and {@provincial} has asked you, in his twenty, what you would do with the province if it were yours, and has said that he asks every student and that the answers tell him more about the men than about the province, and has looked at his watch, since the next brother is at the door.

choices.label: Say you would keep the studium open at any cost
choices.outcome: He says every student says that, and that the ones who mean it become professors, and that the province needs preachers more, and writes something, and you cannot tell whether it was a good answer.

choices.label: Say you would send every man to preach who could, and close what stood in the way
choices.outcome: He puts down the pen. He says that is what he would do, and cannot, and asks what you would close, and you name a house, and it is a house he was prior of, and he laughs, and it is on the file in his own hand.

choices.label: Say you would ask him, since he knows the province and you do not
choices.outcome: He says that is the humblest answer he has had and the least useful, and that a student brother should have an opinion by the third year, and asks again, and you give one, and it is the one you had, and he nods.

events.title: The Habit on Campus
events.body: The studium's students take two courses a year at the secular university across the road, in the habit, since the prior insists on it, and in the seminar on the philosophy of religion the professor has asked you, on the first day, whether you would prefer not to be called Brother, since it might affect how the class receives your arguments. Eleven students are looking at you. Two of them are smiling. The professor means it kindly.

choices.label: Say Brother is your name, and the arguments will have to manage
choices.outcome: The arguments manage. By the fourth week the class calls you Brother without the smile, and by the end of term one of the two who smiled has come to the priory church on a Sunday, alone, and sat at the back.

choices.label: Say your first name will do, in the seminar
choices.outcome: The seminar is easier. The arguments are received as arguments. The prior, told, says nothing, and the master of students says a Dominican in a seminar is a Dominican in a seminar whatever he is called, and you are not sure he is right.

choices.label: Ask the class what they would prefer
choices.outcome: They are embarrassed and then honest, and it is a conversation about what a habit means to eleven people who have never spoken to one, and it is the best class of the term, and the professor gives you the last week's seminar to run.

events.title: The Brother in the Infirmary
events.body: {@confrere} has been ill for a month, the kind of ill the studium does not have a rota for: not dying, not well, in the infirmary at the end of the corridor with the door open and nobody going in, since student brothers are busy and the professed have forgotten he is there. The master of students has said at chapter that the house should remember him. Nobody has. You have a paper due Friday and a stall in choir and the corridor goes past his door.

choices.label: Go in every day, and bring the lectures
choices.outcome: You bring the lectures and read them to him and he passes the term from the bed, and the paper is late, and the master of students, told why, says the paper can wait and the brother could not, and the house is a little ashamed of itself.

choices.label: Go in once, on Sunday, with the newspaper
choices.outcome: He is glad. Once is what the house does. He is well by Lent and says nothing about the month, and years later, at a chapter, he says you came on a Sunday, which he remembered, and you had not.

choices.label: Make a rota, and put it on the board
choices.outcome: The rota fills. The house is ashamed and then dutiful. He is visited every day by a different man and by you on Thursdays, and he says afterward that the rota was the thing that made him feel like a brother and not a patient.
